whyCorrect: Let c be the grams of coarser grade; then the finer grade is 40 − c grams. Cost: 9(40 − c) + 14c = 470, so 360 + 5c = 470 and 5c = 110, giving c = 22. Check: 18 grams at $9 is $162 and 22 grams at $14 is $308, and 162 + 308 = 470.

whyWrong.A: 16 grams of coarser grade means 24 grams of finer, costing 24(9) + 16(14) = $440 — $30 short of $470.
whyWrong.B: 18 is the mass of the finer grade in the correct blend. The question asks for the coarser grade, which is the other 22 grams.
whyWrong.C: An even 20/20 split costs 20(9) + 20(14) = $460, still $10 short. Because the blend costs more than the $11.75 per gram an even split would give, the coarser grade must be over half.

commonMistakes: Solving correctly and then reporting the variable you eliminated instead of the one asked for.
tips: Write down which letter stands for which grade before you solve, then reread the question before choosing.

whyCorrect: The snout moved 1,240 − 1,096 = 144 metres in 2017 − 2005 = 12 years, so the rate is 144 ÷ 12 = 12 metres per year. From 1,240 metres it needs another 1,396 − 1,240 = 156 metres, and 156 ÷ 12 = 13 more years, so 2017 + 13 = 2030.

whyWrong.A: By 2026 the snout is only 1,240 + 12(9) = 1,348 metres out — 48 metres short of 1,396.
whyWrong.B: By 2028 it is 1,240 + 12(11) = 1,372 metres out, still 24 metres short.
whyWrong.D: By 2032 it is 1,240 + 12(15) = 1,420 metres out, 24 metres past the target. Overshooting like this usually means the 156 metres was divided by a rate smaller than 12.

tips: Compute the rate as (change in distance) ÷ (change in years) first, then work forward from whichever data point is closer to the target.

whyCorrect: The racks take 3 × 46 = $138, leaving 540 − 138 = $402. Dividing, 402 ÷ 2.75 = 146.18…, and you cannot buy part of a packet, so round down to 146. Those 146 packets cost $401.50, which fits inside $402.

whyWrong.A: 144 packets cost $396 and leave $6 unspent — enough for two more packets, so this is not the greatest number.
whyWrong.C: 148 packets cost 148(2.75) = $407, which is $5 more than the $402 available.
whyWrong.D: 150 packets cost $412.50, $10.50 over budget. Rounding 146.18 up instead of down is what produces answers above the limit.

commonMistakes: Rounding the quotient up. On a "greatest number you can buy" question the leftover money is always discarded.
tips: Subtract the fixed costs first, then divide — and always round down.

whyCorrect: Together the pumps deliver 4,320 ÷ 24 = 180 cubic metres per minute. If the smaller pump moves x cubic metres per minute, the larger moves 5x, so x + 5x = 180, giving 6x = 180 and x = 30. The larger pump moves 150, and 30 + 150 = 180.

whyWrong.A: 25 for the smaller pump makes the larger 125, a combined 150 per minute — only 3,600 cubic metres in 24 minutes.
whyWrong.C: 36 is 180 ÷ 5. That splits the flow into five parts instead of six; "5 times as much" means the two pumps together account for 1 + 5 = 6 equal parts.
whyWrong.D: 45 is 180 ÷ 4, which treats "5 times as much" as a difference of 4 parts rather than a total of 6.

tips: Convert the ratio into a total number of equal parts (here 1 + 5 = 6) before dividing.

whyCorrect: Substitute the known point: \(T(7)=18-7r=12.4\), so 7r = 5.6 and r = 0.8 degrees per hour. Then \(T(15)=18-0.8(15)=18-12=6\).

whyWrong.A: 4.4 is 12.4 − 0.8(10): it counts 10 more hours after the 7-hour reading instead of the 8 hours from t = 7 to t = 15.
whyWrong.B: 5.2 is 12.4 − 0.8(9), one hour too many past the 7-hour reading (or 18 − 0.8(16)).
whyWrong.D: 7.2 comes from a slip in 5.6 ÷ 7, using r = 0.72 instead of 0.8: 18 − 0.72(15) = 7.2.

tips: Find the constant from the given point first, then evaluate at the new time from t = 0 rather than stepping forward from the data point.

whyCorrect: The balloon fell 1,860 − 1,410 = 450 metres between minute 4 and minute 10, that is 450 ÷ 6 = 75 metres per minute. The start of the descent is 4 minutes before the first reading, so add: 1,860 + 4(75) = 2,160.

whyWrong.A: 1,935 is 1,860 + 75, backing up only 1 minute instead of 4.
whyWrong.B: 2,010 is 1,860 + 2(75), backing up 2 minutes.
whyWrong.C: 2,085 is 1,860 + 3(75), backing up 3 minutes — an off-by-one in counting back from minute 4 to minute 0.

commonMistakes: Subtracting instead of adding. Going backward in time on a descent means the altitude was higher, not lower.
tips: Check your answer by running the model forward: 2,160 − 75(4) = 1,860 and 2,160 − 75(10) = 1,410.

whyCorrect: Clear the denominator first: \(5Y=3m-2w\). Then add 2w to both sides to isolate the m term, \(5Y+2w=3m\), and divide by 3 to get \(m=\frac{5Y+2w}{3}\).

whyWrong.B: Subtracting 2w instead of adding it. The original has −2w on the right, so it must be added to both sides to move it.
whyWrong.C: Divides by 15 instead of multiplying by 5 then dividing by 3 — the 5 was moved to the wrong side of the equation.
whyWrong.D: Keeps both the 5 in the numerator and a 15 in the denominator, which multiplies the denominators 5 and 3 together instead of clearing the 5 first.

tips: Undo the division before you undo the subtraction; solving for a variable follows the reverse of the order of operations.

whyCorrect: The graph of \(P(b)=-25b^{2}+900b-3{,}200\) is a downward parabola, so the greatest profit is at the vertex, \(b=-\frac{900}{2(-25)}=\frac{900}{50}=18\). The maximum profit itself is P(18) = $4,900.

whyWrong.A: P(16) = $4,800, less than P(18). 16 and 20 sit the same distance either side of the vertex, which is why they give the same profit.
whyWrong.C: P(20) = $4,800, also below the maximum. Being close to the vertex is not being at it.
whyWrong.D: 36 is \(\frac{900}{25}\), which forgets the 2 in \(-\frac{b}{2a}\). At 36 blades P(36) = −$3,200, a loss.

tips: For a quadratic, the maximising input is \(-\frac{b}{2a}\); the value of the maximum is what you get by substituting it back.

whyCorrect: Let the width be w, so the height is w + 7 and \(w(w+7)=330\), that is \(w^{2}+7w-330=0\). Factor as (w + 22)(w − 15) = 0, so w = 15 and the height is 22. The perimeter is 2(15 + 22) = 74.

whyWrong.A: 66 is the perimeter of an 11-by-22 rectangle, whose area is 242, not 330.
whyWrong.C: 78 is the perimeter of a 16-by-23 rectangle — the sides differ by 7 but the area is 368.
whyWrong.D: 82 uses the factor pair 11 and 30. Their product is 330, but they differ by 19, not by the required 7.

commonMistakes: Stopping at w = 15 and choosing the side length instead of the perimeter.
tips: When you guess a factor pair of the area, check the difference between the two numbers before using it.

whyCorrect: Square the numerator completely: \((4a^{3}b)^{2}=16a^{6}b^{2}\) — the exponent 2 hits the 4 as well. Then divide: \(\frac{16a^{6}b^{2}}{8ab^{4}}=2a^{6-1}b^{2-4}=2a^{5}b^{-2}=\frac{2a^{5}}{b^{2}}\).

whyWrong.B: Leaves \(a^{6}\), forgetting to subtract the single a in the denominator: \(a^{6}\div a=a^{5}\).
whyWrong.C: Has \(\frac{1}{2}\) instead of 2; 16 ÷ 8 = 2, not \(\frac{8}{16}\).
whyWrong.D: Puts \(b^{2}\) in the numerator. Since \(b^{2}\div b^{4}=b^{-2}\), the b must end up in the denominator.

tips: Apply the outer exponent to every factor inside the parentheses, coefficient included, before dividing.

whyCorrect: Losing 3% of what is present at the start of each month leaves 97% of it, so the amount is \(250(0.97)^{8}\). Since \((0.97)^{8}\approx0.7837\), the mass is about 195.9, which rounds to 196 grams.

whyWrong.A: 184 is \(250(0.97)^{10}\) — two months too many in the exponent.
whyWrong.B: 190 is what you get by removing 3% of the original 250 grams every month: 7.5 × 8 = 60, and 250 − 60 = 190. The percentage applies to the shrinking amount, not the starting amount.
whyWrong.C: 194 comes from rounding \((0.97)^{8}\) too early (using about 0.776 instead of 0.7837). Keep the full power until the last step.

commonMistakes: Treating a percentage decrease as a fixed amount each period; that is linear, not exponential.
tips: A repeated percent loss of r gives a multiplier of 1 − r raised to the number of periods.

whyCorrect: Two numbers with sum 30 and product 200 are the roots of \(x^{2}-30x+200=0\), which factors as (x − 10)(x − 20) = 0. So the two masses are 10 and 20 kilograms; since there is more sugar than peel, the sugar is 20.

whyWrong.A: 10 is the mass of the peel — the smaller of the two roots, and the batch is stated to have more sugar than peel.
whyWrong.B: 15 splits the 30 evenly, but 15 × 15 = 225, not 200.
whyWrong.D: 25 pairs with 5 to give a product of 125, and it pairs with 8 to give 200 but a sum of 33. No pair containing 25 satisfies both conditions.

tips: A sum and a product turn straight into a quadratic: \(x^{2}-(\text{sum})x+(\text{product})=0\).

whyCorrect: Put both cloth lengths in the same unit: 1.4 metres is 140 centimetres. That is 140 ÷ 8 = 17.5 lots of 8 centimetres, and each lot needs 3 metres of warp, so 17.5 × 3 = 52.5 metres.

whyWrong.A: 37.5 divides the 3 metres (300 cm) by 8 — the wrong quantity is being divided. Check it: 37.5 metres of warp makes only 100 cm of cloth.
whyWrong.B: 42 comes from dividing 140 by 10 rather than 8; 42 metres of warp makes only 112 cm of cloth.
whyWrong.C: 48 metres of warp makes 48 ÷ 3 × 8 = 128 cm of cloth, not the required 140 cm.

commonMistakes: Mixing metres and centimetres in the same ratio.
tips: Convert units before setting up the proportion, then check by running the ratio backward from your answer.

whyCorrect: Multiply the rate by the density to get kilograms per hour: 0.9 × 400 = 360. Over 7 hours that is 360 × 7 = 2,520 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 2,160 is 360 × 6, a six-hour day rather than the stated seven.
whyWrong.C: 2,800 is 400 × 7, which uses the density as though the cutter lifted a full cubic metre each hour and drops the 0.9 entirely.
whyWrong.D: 3,150 works out to 450 kilograms an hour. Because 0.9 cubic metres is less than one cubic metre, the hourly mass has to be less than 400 kilograms, so any answer built on a larger rate is going the wrong way.

tips: Track the units: (m³ per hour) × (kg per m³) × (hours) leaves kilograms.

whyCorrect: The pay gap depends only on the mass gap. The most picked is Bilqis's 24.0 kg and the least is Chandra's 15.5 kg, a difference of 8.5 kg. At $1.80 per kilogram, 8.5 × 1.80 = $15.30.

whyWrong.A: $12.60 is 7 × $1.80, a 7 kg gap — it comes from misreading one of the two extreme entries.
whyWrong.B: $14.40 is 8 × $1.80, the gap you get by rounding Chandra's 15.5 up to 16.
whyWrong.D: $16.20 is 9 × $1.80, the gap from rounding 15.5 down to 15.

tips: Subtract the masses first and multiply once, rather than computing both wages and subtracting.

whyCorrect: The first 9 joints total 9 × 62 = 558 mm. All 10 must total 10 × 63 = 630 mm. The tenth joint is 630 − 558 = 72 mm. Equivalently, raising the mean by 1 mm across 10 joints needs 10 extra millimetres above the old mean: 62 + 10 = 72.

whyWrong.A: 64 is 63 + 1, adding the 1 mm rise once. The extra millimetre has to be supplied for every one of the 10 joints, not just the new one.
whyWrong.B: 66 gives a total of 558 + 66 = 624 mm and a mean of 62.4 mm, not 63.
whyWrong.C: 70 comes from rounding 9 × 62 = 558 to 560 before subtracting from 630; it leaves the mean at 62.8 mm.

commonMistakes: Averaging 62 and 63 in some way instead of working with totals.
tips: On any changing-mean question, convert each mean to a total (mean × count) and subtract.

whyCorrect: Angles in corresponding positions at two parallel lines cut by a transversal are equal, so 4x + 16 = 6x − 14. That gives 30 = 2x and x = 15. The angle measure is 4(15) + 16 = 76 degrees, and the check 6(15) − 14 = 76 agrees.

whyWrong.A: 15 is the value of x, not the angle. You still have to substitute it back into one of the expressions.
whyWrong.B: 46 is 4(15) − 14, mixing the coefficient from one expression with the constant from the other.
whyWrong.C: 62 is 4(15) + 2, a slip in adding the 16.

commonMistakes: Setting corresponding angles supplementary. Corresponding angles at parallel lines are equal; it is same-side interior angles that add to 180 degrees.
tips: Substitute your x into both expressions — if they do not match, the setup was wrong.

whyCorrect: The 45 metres along the ground is the side adjacent to the 52-degree angle and the height is the side opposite it. Opposite over adjacent is tangent, so \(\tan 52^{\circ}=\frac{h}{45}\) and \(h=45\tan 52^{\circ}\).

whyWrong.B: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so \(45\sin 52^{\circ}\) would require the 45 to be the slanted line of sight, not the ground distance.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{45}{\tan 52^{\circ}}\) inverts the ratio; it would find the ground distance from a known height. It also gives a height under 45 m, though a 52-degree elevation must give a height greater than the base distance.
whyWrong.D: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so this again treats 45 as the hypotenuse.

tips: Label which side is opposite and which is adjacent to the given angle before choosing the ratio.

whyCorrect: The full cylinder holds \(\pi r^{2}h=\pi(1.5)^{2}(2.4)=5.4\pi\) cubic metres. Filled to 80%, the water is \(0.8(5.4\pi)=4.32\pi\), so V = 4.32.

whyWrong.A: 3.24 is 0.6 × 5.4, using 60% instead of 80% (equivalently, taking away 40%).
whyWrong.C: 5.4 is the cistern's full capacity — the 80% was never applied.
whyWrong.D: 10.8 is twice the full capacity. Water filling part of the cistern must give a value below 5.4.

tips: Compute the whole volume first, then take the percentage; the \(\pi\) can be carried along untouched.

whyCorrect: With c the price per kilogram of cardamom and v that of cloves, 3c + 5v = 196 and 5c + 2v = 181. Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 5 to match the v terms: 6c + 10v = 392 and 25c + 10v = 905. Subtracting gives 19c = 513, so c = 27 (and v = 23, which checks: 5(27) + 2(23) = 181).
commonMistakes: Solving the system correctly and then reporting the price of cloves, 23.
tips: Eliminate the variable you are not asked about — here the cloves — so the first result you reach is the one you need.

whyCorrect: Substitute v = 30 into \(d(v)=\frac{v^{2}}{20}+\frac{v}{2}\): the first term is \(\frac{30^{2}}{20}=\frac{900}{20}=45\) and the second is \(\frac{30}{2}=15\). Adding, d(30) = 60 metres.
commonMistakes: Squaring after dividing — computing \(\left(\frac{30}{20}\right)^{2}\) instead of \(\frac{30^{2}}{20}\).
tips: Square first, then divide; the exponent applies only to v.

whyCorrect: The ruler and the cliff subtend the same angle at the eye, so the two triangles are similar and corresponding sides are proportional: \(\frac{\text{cliff height}}{400}=\frac{30}{60}\). Since \(\frac{30}{60}=\frac{1}{2}\), the cliff is \(\frac{1}{2}(400)=200\) metres tall.
commonMistakes: Mixing units inside the ratio. The 30 and 60 are both centimetres, so their ratio is unitless and can multiply a distance in metres directly.
tips: Set up the proportion as (small height)/(small distance) = (large height)/(large distance) and keep each pair in the same units.

whyCorrect: Each tent contributes the same $14, so the number of tents is 322 ÷ 14 = 23. Check by multiplying back: 14 × 23 = 322.

whyWrong.B: 25 tents would bring in 14 × 25 = $350, which is $28 more than she took.
whyWrong.C: 28 tents would bring in $392.
whyWrong.D: 32 tents would bring in $448; 32 is roughly 322 ÷ 10, so it comes from dividing by the wrong number.

tips: Multiply your answer by the per-unit price to confirm it reproduces the total.

whyCorrect: The same amount each day means the total splits evenly: 546 ÷ 7 = 78 minutes. Check: 78 × 7 = 546.

whyWrong.A: 76 minutes a day totals 532 minutes over 7 days, 14 short.
whyWrong.C: 82 minutes a day totals 574 minutes, 28 too many.
whyWrong.D: 91 is 546 ÷ 6 — six days instead of the stated seven.

tips: Confirm by multiplying back; a division answer is only right if it rebuilds the total.

whyCorrect: Substitute h = 4 into \(C=18+7h\): the hourly part is 7(4) = 28 and the flat $18 is added once, so C = 18 + 28 = 46.

whyWrong.A: 25 is 18 + 7, which charges for only one hour.
whyWrong.C: 72 is 18 × 4; the $18 is a one-time charge, not a per-hour rate.
whyWrong.D: 100 is (18 + 7)(4), adding before multiplying. Order of operations requires 7h first.

tips: In C = (fixed) + (rate)(time), only the rate gets multiplied by the time.

whyCorrect: Substitute t = 3 into \(L(t)=45-9t\): 9(3) = 27, and 45 − 27 = 18 kilometres still uncleared.

whyWrong.B: 27 is the number of kilometres the plough has cleared, which is what 9t alone gives. The function reports what is left.
whyWrong.C: 36 is 45 − 9, which uses t = 1 instead of t = 3.
whyWrong.D: 45 is L(0), the length before the plough started.

commonMistakes: Reading 9t as the answer instead of subtracting it from 45.
tips: Check what the function is defined to output — here it is the road still uncleared, not the distance covered.

whyCorrect: "Fewer than 9" means strictly below 9, so 9 itself is not allowed. That is the strict inequality \(n<9\).

whyWrong.A: \(n>9\) reverses the direction and would allow 10 or more climbers, which the notice forbids.
whyWrong.B: \(n\ge 9\) also points the wrong way and permits 9 or more.
whyWrong.D: \(n\le 9\) points the right way but includes 9; "fewer than" excludes the boundary value. "At most 9" is what \(\le\) means.

tips: "Fewer/less than" and "more than" are strict (< and >); "at most" and "at least" include the boundary (\(\le\) and \(\ge\)).

whyCorrect: Set the output to 180 and solve for the input: 24h = 180, so h = 180 ÷ 24 = 7.5 hours.

whyWrong.A: 6 hours gives 24(6) = 144 metres, 36 short.
whyWrong.C: 9 hours gives 24(9) = 216 metres, well past 180.
whyWrong.D: 156 is 180 − 24, subtracting the rate instead of dividing by it.

commonMistakes: Substituting 180 for h and computing 24(180). Here 180 is the output, so it belongs on the left side of the equation.
tips: Ask whether the given number is an input or an output before you substitute.

whyCorrect: Distribute the 4 across both terms in the parentheses: 4(3n) = 12n and 4(−7) = −28, giving 12n − 28. Then add the 5n: 12n + 5n = 17n, so the expression is 17n − 28.

whyWrong.A: 8n − 28 comes from multiplying only the −7 by the 4 and leaving 3n untouched: 3n + 5n = 8n.
whyWrong.B: 12n − 28 stops after distributing and never adds the 5n.
whyWrong.D: 17n − 7 distributes the 4 to the 3n but not to the −7; \(4\times(-7)=-28\).

tips: The factor outside parentheses multiplies every term inside, constants included.

whyCorrect: Total plums is plums per layer times number of layers: \(x^{4}\cdot x^{2}\). Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, so the total is \(x^{4+2}=x^{6}\).

whyWrong.A: \(x^{2}\) is just the number of layers; it never multiplies by the plums in each layer.
whyWrong.C: \(x^{8}\) multiplies the exponents (4 × 2). Exponents multiply when a power is raised to a power, as in \((x^{4})^{2}\), not when two powers are multiplied.
whyWrong.D: \(2x^{6}\) adds a factor of 2 that nothing in the problem produces; adding exponents does not create a coefficient.

tips: \(x^{a}\cdot x^{b}=x^{a+b}\), but \((x^{a})^{b}=x^{ab}\) — keep the two rules apart.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 7 into \(T(d)=d^{2}+5\): \(7^{2}=49\), then 49 + 5 = 54 minutes.

whyWrong.A: 12 is 7 + 5, which ignores the square altogether.
whyWrong.B: 19 is 2(7) + 5, treating \(d^{2}\) as 2d. Squaring means \(7\times 7\), not \(7\times 2\).
whyWrong.D: 61 is 56 + 5, from an arithmetic slip in \(7^{2}\).

tips: Square before adding; the exponent binds tighter than the addition.

whyCorrect: Substitute w = 4 into \(A(w)=3(2)^{w}\): \(2^{4}=16\), then 3 × 16 = 48 square metres. In words, the mat starts at 3 and doubles four times: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48.

whyWrong.A: 24 is 3 × 2 × 4, multiplying by the exponent instead of raising to it (and it is only three doublings).
whyWrong.B: 32 is \(2\cdot 2^{4}\) — starting the doubling from 2 rather than the given 3 square metres.
whyWrong.D: 81 is \(3^{4}\), swapping the base and the coefficient. The 3 is the starting area; the 2 is the growth factor.

tips: In \(a(b)^{w}\), a is the starting amount and b is what it gets multiplied by each period.

whyCorrect: Add 9 to both sides: \(p^{2}=49\). Taking the positive square root, p = 7. The problem says p is positive, so the negative root is rejected.

whyWrong.C: 24.5 is 49 ÷ 2, dividing by 2 instead of taking a square root.
whyWrong.D: 49 is the value of \(p^{2}\); the last step, taking the square root, was skipped.

tips: Isolate the squared term first, then take the square root — and check the sign restriction stated in the problem.

whyCorrect: The tile count is length times width, \((x+4)(x-9)\). Expanding: \(x^{2}-9x+4x-36\), and the two middle terms combine to −5x, giving \(x^{2}-5x-36\).

whyWrong.A: \(x^{2}-13x-36\) treats both middle terms as negative (−9x − 4x). The +4 keeps its sign when it multiplies x.
whyWrong.C: \(x^{2}+5x-36\) has the middle term's sign flipped; since 9 is larger than 4, −9x + 4x is negative.
whyWrong.D: \(x^{2}-36\) uses the difference-of-squares shortcut, which only applies to \((x+a)(x-a)\) with the same number. Here 4 and 9 differ, so the middle term does not cancel.

tips: Expand all four products, then combine — the middle terms cancel only when the two constants are opposites.

whyCorrect: 14 litres is 7 times the 2 litres in the recipe, so the madder scales by the same factor: 5 × 7 = 35 grams. Equivalently, \(\frac{5}{2}=\frac{m}{14}\) gives 2m = 70 and m = 35.

whyWrong.A: 17.5 applies the 2 twice — halving the 14 litres to 7 and then multiplying by the 2.5 grams-per-litre rate.
whyWrong.B: 28 is 14 × 2, using the litres figure from the recipe as though it were a grams-per-litre rate.
whyWrong.D: 70 is 14 × 5, which treats the recipe as 5 grams per litre and ignores that those 5 grams serve 2 litres.

tips: Find the scale factor between the two known quantities (14 ÷ 2 = 7) and apply it once.

whyCorrect: 35% of 420 is 0.35 × 420. Split it if that helps: 10% is 42, so 30% is 126, and 5% is 21, giving 126 + 21 = 147.

whyWrong.A: 120 is 420 ÷ 3.5 — dividing by the percentage instead of multiplying by its decimal form.
whyWrong.B: 126 is 30% of 420; the extra 5% (21 lanterns) is missing.
whyWrong.C: 140 is one third of 420, that is 33\(\frac{1}{3}\)%, not 35%.

tips: Convert the percent to a decimal and multiply; check by seeing that 35% should land between a quarter (105) and a half (210).

whyCorrect: Add all three rows: 128 + 155 = 283, then 283 + 96 = 379 nesting pairs.

whyWrong.A: 251 is 155 + 96, leaving out Craigan's 128.
whyWrong.B: 283 is 128 + 155, leaving out Bo Rua's 96.
whyWrong.C: 341 falls 38 short of the true total — a carrying error. Add two numbers at a time and keep the columns aligned.

tips: Estimate first: three values near 130, 155 and 100 must total well over 350, which rules out the two-value sums immediately.

whyCorrect: The mean is the total divided by the count. The six values sum to 4 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 9 = 36, and 36 ÷ 6 = 6 eggs per nest.

whyWrong.A: 4.5 is far below even the middle of the data; the sum 36 divided by 6 is 6, and 4.5 would need a total of 27.
whyWrong.B: 5 is the mode — the value that appears most often — not the mean.
whyWrong.C: 5.5 is the median: the average of the two middle values, 5 and 6, once the list is in order.

commonMistakes: Answering with the median or mode when the question asks for the mean.
tips: Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle value; mode = most frequent. Check which one the question names.

whyCorrect: The three angles of a triangle total 180 degrees, and the right angle uses 90 of them. That leaves 90 degrees for the two acute angles together, so the other one is 90 − 37 = 53.

whyWrong.A: 43 comes from subtracting 37 from 80 instead of 90.
whyWrong.C: 63 comes from subtracting 37 from 100.
whyWrong.D: 143 is 180 − 37, which forgets that the right angle has already taken 90 of the 180 degrees.

tips: In a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary — they add to 90, not 180.

whyCorrect: The sections are identical, so the floor area is 6 × 2.5 = 15 square metres.

whyWrong.A: 7.5 is 3 × 2.5, counting only half of the six sections.
whyWrong.B: 12.5 is 5 × 2.5, one section short.
whyWrong.D: 18 is 6 × 3, from rounding the 2.5 square metres up to 3 before multiplying.

tips: Multiply before rounding; rounding first throws the total off by six times the rounding error here.

whyCorrect: The area of a circle is \(\pi r^{2}\). With r = 6, that is \(\pi(6)^{2}=36\pi\), so k = 36.

whyWrong.A: 6 is the radius itself, not its square.
whyWrong.B: 12 is 2r; \(2\pi r=12\pi\) is the pond's circumference, not its area.
whyWrong.C: 24 is 4 × 6; squaring 6 gives 36, not 24.

tips: Area uses \(r^{2}\) and comes out in square metres; circumference uses 2r and comes out in metres.

whyCorrect: Equal shares means dividing: 4.5 ÷ 6 = 0.75 litres per mould. Check by multiplying back: 0.75 × 6 = 4.5.
commonMistakes: Dividing 6 by 4.5 and entering 1.33; the smaller quantity is being split among the larger number of moulds, so each share must be less than 1 litre.
tips: Either 0.75 or 3/4 is accepted — enter whichever is easier to type without rounding.

whyCorrect: Substitute t = 6 into \(a(t)=5t^{2}\). Square first: \(6^{2}=36\). Then multiply by 5: 5 × 36 = 180 metres.
commonMistakes: Computing \((5\cdot 6)^{2}=900\). The 5 is a coefficient, so only t is squared.
tips: Exponents come before multiplication in the order of operations.

whyCorrect: The right angle is at E, so the two legs are DE = 8 and EF = 15 and the hypotenuse is DF. Viewed from angle D, the side opposite is EF = 15 and the side adjacent is DE = 8, so \(\tan D=\frac{15}{8}\) (1.875 is accepted too).
commonMistakes: Entering \(\frac{8}{15}\), which is \(\tan F\) — the same two legs, but opposite and adjacent swap when you change which acute angle you stand at.
tips: Find the right angle first; the two sides touching it are the legs, and the one not touching your angle is the opposite side.

whyCorrect: Lines that never meet are parallel, so their slopes are equal. Solving the second equation for y gives \(y=\frac{3}{m}x-\frac{25}{m}\), so \(\frac{3}{m}=\frac{3}{5}\) and m = 5. The intercepts differ (−5 against −4), so the lines really are parallel and not the same line.

whyWrong.A: m = −5 gives slope \(-\frac{3}{5}\) — the right size but the wrong sign, so the lines cross.
whyWrong.B: m = 3 gives slope \(\frac{3}{3}=1\), not \(\frac{3}{5}\). Matching m to the coefficient of x is not the same as matching slopes.
whyWrong.D: m = 9 gives slope \(\frac{3}{9}=\frac{1}{3}\).

tips: Put both lines in \(y=mx+b\) form before comparing; parallel needs equal slopes and different intercepts.

whyCorrect: b is the rate: \(b=\frac{51-27}{14-6}=\frac{24}{8}=3\) francs per kilometre. Then a = 27 − 3(6) = 9. So a + b = 9 + 3 = 12.

whyWrong.A: 9 is the value of a alone — the fixed part of the fare, with b never added.
whyWrong.C: 15 is 9 + 6, keeping the correct a but dividing the 24-franc difference by 4 instead of by the 8-kilometre gap.
whyWrong.D: 21 is 27 − 6, subtracting the 6 kilometres straight from the 27 francs. The 6 has to be multiplied by b first.

tips: Two points give the rate by (change in output) ÷ (change in input); substitute back to get the constant term.

whyCorrect: With c children, the adults number 17 − c, so the takings are 32(17 − c) + 19c = 544 − 13c. Requiring at least $460 gives \(544-13c\ge 460\), so \(13c\le 84\) and \(c\le 6.46\). The greatest whole number of children is 6, which brings in $466.

whyWrong.A: 5 children gives $479, which clears the target, but 6 also clears it, so 5 is not the greatest.
whyWrong.C: 7 children gives 544 − 91 = $453, which is $7 short of the $460 minimum.
whyWrong.D: 8 children gives $440, $20 short.

commonMistakes: Rounding 6.46 up. Because each extra child lowers the takings, the count must be rounded down to stay above the minimum.
tips: Express the takings in one variable first; the coefficient −13 tells you what each swap from adult to child costs.

whyCorrect: Work in rates. If the smaller gate takes t hours, it drains \(\frac{1}{t}\) of the pond per hour and the larger drains \(\frac{1}{t-5}\). Together they do \(\frac{1}{6}\) per hour: \(\frac{1}{t}+\frac{1}{t-5}=\frac{1}{6}\). Multiplying through by 6t(t − 5) gives \(t^{2}-17t+30=0\), so t = 15 or t = 2; t = 2 is impossible since t − 5 must be positive, leaving t = 15.

whyWrong.A: 10 is the larger gate's time (15 − 5). The question asks for the smaller gate.
whyWrong.B: 12 for the smaller means 7 for the larger; those rates combine to about 4.4 hours, faster than the stated 6.
whyWrong.D: 18 for the smaller means 13 for the larger, which combine to about 7.6 hours, slower than the stated 6.

commonMistakes: Adding the times instead of the rates. Two gates never take longer together than either alone.
tips: Add the per-hour fractions, not the hours, then check that the combined time falls between half the faster time and the faster time itself.

whyCorrect: Feed p into q: \(q(p(x))=(2x-5)^{2}+1\). Expand the square in full: \((2x-5)^{2}=4x^{2}-20x+25\), and adding 1 gives \(4x^{2}-20x+26\).

whyWrong.A: \(4x^{2}+26\) squares each term separately, dropping the −20x cross term. \((a-b)^{2}\) is \(a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}\), not \(a^{2}+b^{2}\).
whyWrong.B: \(2x^{2}-3\) is \(p(q(x))\) — the treatments applied in the reverse order.
whyWrong.C: \(4x^{2}-20x+24\) subtracts the 1 instead of adding it; q adds 1 to whatever it receives.

tips: Write the composition as \(q(\text{whole expression})\) in brackets first, then expand — that keeps the cross term from disappearing.

whyCorrect: A negative exponent in the denominator moves up: \(\frac{x^{8}}{y^{-4}}=x^{8}y^{4}\), so the expression is \((16x^{8}y^{4})^{3/4}\). Apply the \(\frac{3}{4}\) power to each factor: \(16^{3/4}=(2^{4})^{3/4}=2^{3}=8\), \(x^{8\cdot 3/4}=x^{6}\), and \(y^{4\cdot 3/4}=y^{3}\), giving \(8x^{6}y^{3}\).

whyWrong.B: 12 is \(16\times\frac{3}{4}\). The exponent raises the 16 to a power; it does not multiply it.
whyWrong.C: \(x^{11}\) adds the exponents (8 + 3). A power of a power multiplies them: \(8\times\frac{3}{4}=6\).
whyWrong.D: 64 is \(4^{3}\), which takes the square root of 16 before cubing. The denominator 4 in \(\frac{3}{4}\) calls for the fourth root, which is 2.

tips: Read \(a^{m/n}\) as "the n-th root, then the m-th power" and apply it separately to the coefficient and each variable.

whyCorrect: Touching the x-axis at exactly one point means the quadratic has one repeated root, so the discriminant is zero: \(b^{2}-4(2)(18)=0\), giving \(b^{2}=144\) and b = ±12. Since b is stated to be positive, b = 12.

whyWrong.A: 6 comes from using \(b^{2}=2\times 18=36\) and forgetting the factor of 4 in \(4ac\).
whyWrong.B: 9 is half of the constant 18; the constant does not transfer to b that way.
whyWrong.D: 18 sets b equal to the constant term. Check it: \(18^{2}-4(2)(18)=324-144=180\), a positive discriminant, so that parabola would cross the axis twice.

tips: One x-intercept means discriminant = 0, two means positive, none means negative.

whyCorrect: Factor both parts: the numerator is a difference of squares, \(x^{2}-9=(x-3)(x+3)\), and the denominator factors as \(x^{2}+x-12=(x+4)(x-3)\) since 4 and −3 multiply to −12 and add to 1. The common factor (x − 3) cancels, leaving \(\frac{x+3}{x+4}\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{x-3}{x-4}\) cancels the wrong pair — it keeps (x − 3) instead of cancelling it and mis-signs the denominator's factors.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{x+4}\) cancels the x terms out of \(\frac{x+3}{x+4}\). You may only cancel whole factors, never individual terms of a sum.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{x+3}{x-4}\) factors the denominator as (x − 4)(x + 3), but that expands to \(x^{2}-x-12\), with the wrong middle sign.

tips: Multiply your factored denominator back out to check the middle term before cancelling.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{2}\) would put the curve at \(\frac{1}{2}(36)-12=6\) when x = 10, not 15.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{4}{3}\) is the reciprocal — it comes from dividing 36 by 27 instead of 27 by 36.
whyWrong.D: 3 comes from dividing 27 by 9 rather than 36, a slip in squaring 10 − 4. Checking, 3(36) − 12 = 96, far from 15.

tips: Substitute the point and solve for the single unknown; then plug your value back in to confirm the point lies on the curve.

whyCorrect: Set them equal: \(x^{2}-4x+7=2x+c\), which rearranges to \(x^{2}-6x+(7-c)=0\). Two crossing points means a positive discriminant: \(36-4(7-c)>0\), so \(8+4c>0\) and c > −2. Of the choices only 1 satisfies that.

whyWrong.A: c = −5 gives discriminant 36 − 4(12) = −12, negative, so the line misses the parabola entirely.
whyWrong.B: c = −3 gives 36 − 4(10) = −4, still negative — no intersection.
whyWrong.C: c = −2 gives exactly 0, the boundary case where the line is tangent and touches at one point only, not two.

tips: Substitute one equation into the other, collect into \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\), and let the discriminant's sign decide the number of intersections.

whyCorrect: No solution means the two lines are parallel with different constants. The x-coefficients scale by 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so the y-coefficient must scale by 2 as well: a = 2(−3) = −6. Then the second equation is 8x − 6y = 1 while doubling the first gives 8x − 6y = 14, so the two can never both hold.

whyWrong.B: a = −3 copies the first equation's coefficient without the factor of 2, leaving slopes \(\frac{4}{3}\) and \(\frac{8}{3}\), which cross at one point.
whyWrong.C: a = 3 flips the sign as well as missing the scaling.
whyWrong.D: a = 6 has the right size but the wrong sign; 8x + 6y = 1 is not parallel to 4x − 3y = 7.

commonMistakes: Checking only that the x-coefficients are proportional. Both variable coefficients must scale by the same factor while the constants do not.
tips: Compare the ratios \(\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}=\frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}}\ne\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}\) for no solution.

whyCorrect: Volunteers were randomly assigned to the two routines, which is what licenses a cause-and-effect claim: random assignment makes the two groups comparable, so a significant difference afterwards is attributable to the treatment. But the volunteers were recruited, not randomly drawn from a population, so the conclusion can only be extended to the people in the study.

whyWrong.A: The study found a significant difference between the groups, which is evidence of a relationship, not evidence against one.
whyWrong.B: This describes people who choose a routine themselves. Self-selection is exactly what random assignment removes, so the study says nothing about it.
whyWrong.C: This generalises to every adult in the country. Because the sample was volunteers rather than a random sample of the country, the result does not transfer to that whole population — and "every" is stronger than any statistical result supports.

tips: Random assignment licenses causal language; random selection licenses generalisation to a population. Check which one the study has.

whyCorrect: With 11 values in order, the median is the 6th, which is 22. The eleven values total 255, so the mean is 255 ÷ 11 ≈ 23.2. The single value of 41 sits far above the rest and pulls the mean upward while leaving the middle value untouched, so the mean exceeds the median.

whyWrong.A: This is the direction an outlier on the low side would produce. The one extreme value here, 41, is high.
whyWrong.B: They are not equal: 23.2 against 22. Equality would need the values to be symmetric about the centre.
whyWrong.D: The mean of 23.2 is below both 24 and 41. A mean always lies between the smallest and largest values.

tips: The median ignores how far away an extreme value is; the mean does not. Spot the outlier and you know which way the mean shifts.

whyCorrect: Track the salt, not the brine. If x litres of the 30% brine are used, the rest is 45 − x litres of the 12% brine, and the salt must balance: 0.30x + 0.12(45 − x) = 0.18(45) = 8.1. That gives 0.18x + 5.4 = 8.1, so 0.18x = 2.7 and x = 15 litres.

whyWrong.A: 12 litres of the 30% brine with 33 litres of the 12% gives 3.6 + 3.96 = 7.56 kg of salt, a 16.8% mixture — the number is copied from a percentage in the problem.
whyWrong.C: 18 litres of the 30% brine gives 5.4 + 3.24 = 8.64 kg of salt, a 19.2% mixture. This copies the target percentage instead of solving for the volume.
whyWrong.D: 30 litres is the amount of the 12% brine used, the other part of the mixture.

commonMistakes: Averaging the two percentages. Since 18% is closer to 12% than to 30%, more of the weaker brine is needed, so the 30% share must be under half of 45.
tips: Write one equation in litres of salt: (concentration)(volume) for each part equals the same for the mixture.

whyCorrect: The suit is chosen from the failed ones only, so the denominator is the number of failures, 13 + 21 = 34, not the whole 180. Of those 34, the 21 from Birch give a probability of \(\frac{21}{34}\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{21}{180}\) is the chance that a suit drawn from all 180 both failed and came from Birch — it ignores the condition that the suit already failed.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{34}{180}\) is the overall failure rate across both workshops, which answers a different question.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{21}{105}\) uses Birch's 105 suits as the denominator. That is the probability a Birch suit failed — the condition reversed.

tips: In a conditional probability, the group named after "given" or "is selected from" becomes the denominator.

whyCorrect: Because \(\overline{ST}\) is parallel to \(\overline{QR}\), triangle PST is similar to triangle PQR, and corresponding sides use the whole sides from P. Here PQ = PS + SQ = 12 + 18 = 30, so the scale factor is \(\frac{PS}{PQ}=\frac{12}{30}=\frac{2}{5}\). Therefore \(ST=\frac{2}{5}(45)=18\).

whyWrong.A: 15 is 45 ÷ 3, treating the scale factor as \(\frac{1}{3}\) rather than \(\frac{12}{30}\).
whyWrong.C: 20 comes from using \(\frac{12}{18}\) as the scale factor and applying it to PQ = 30 instead of to QR = 45. The 18 is only part of PQ, not the full corresponding side.
whyWrong.D: 27 uses \(\frac{SQ}{PQ}=\frac{18}{30}\), which is the leftover part of the side, not the part corresponding to ST.

commonMistakes: Using PS : SQ = 12 : 18 as the ratio. The similar triangles share vertex P, so both corresponding sides must be measured from P.
tips: Add the pieces to get the full side first, then form the ratio (small triangle side) : (large triangle side).

whyCorrect: The sphere holds \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(6)^{3}=\frac{4}{3}\pi(216)=288\pi\) cubic centimetres. Each rod holds \(\pi(2)^{2}(9)=36\pi\). Dividing, \(\frac{288\pi}{36\pi}=8\) rods exactly, with nothing left over.

whyWrong.A: 6 is \(\frac{216\pi}{36\pi}\), which uses \(r^{3}\) alone and drops the \(\frac{4}{3}\) from the sphere's volume formula.
whyWrong.C: 9 is the rod's length in centimetres, not a count of rods.
whyWrong.D: 12 would require each rod to hold only \(24\pi\) cubic centimetres; the rod's radius of 2 must be squared, giving \(\pi(4)(9)=36\pi\).

tips: The \(\pi\) cancels in the division, so leave it symbolic rather than approximating either volume.

whyCorrect: The right angle is at Y, so XY and YZ are the legs and XZ is the hypotenuse: \(XZ=\sqrt{9^{2}+40^{2}}=\sqrt{1681}=41\). Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and the leg adjacent to angle X is XY = 9, so \(\cos X=\frac{9}{41}\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{41}{9}\) inverts the ratio. A cosine can never exceed 1, so a fraction greater than 1 is always wrong here.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{9}{40}\) is opposite over adjacent, which is \(\tan X\).
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{40}{41}\) is opposite over hypotenuse, which is \(\sin X\) (and equals \(\cos Z\)).

tips: Find the hypotenuse first, then label opposite and adjacent relative to the named angle — cosine always uses the hypotenuse.

whyCorrect: With L kilograms of lentils, the beans make up 20 − L kilograms, so the portions come to 6L + 4(20 − L) = 2L + 80. Requiring at least 90 portions gives \(2L+80\ge 90\), so \(L\ge 5\). The least value is 5 kilograms, which yields exactly 90 portions.

whyWrong.B: 6 kilograms of lentils yields 92 portions, which meets the requirement but is not the smallest amount that does.
whyWrong.C: 8 kilograms yields 96 portions — comfortably over, and 3 kilograms more than needed.
whyWrong.D: 10 kilograms yields 100 portions, the answer to "how many for 100 portions", not the minimum for 90.

commonMistakes: Reading "at least 90 portions" as "exactly 90 is not allowed". At least includes equality, so 5 qualifies.
tips: Reduce to one variable using the fixed 20 kg total, then solve the inequality — the boundary value itself is usually the answer.

whyCorrect: Let the second leg be s. The first is 3s and the third is 3s − 400. Their total is s + 3s + (3s − 400) = 7s − 400 = 3,800, so 7s = 4,200 and s = 600. Check: 1,800 + 600 + 1,400 = 3,800.
commonMistakes: Defining the variable as the first runner's leg; that leaves you dividing by 3 at the end and makes the third leg awkward to write.
tips: Name the smallest quantity as the variable so every other quantity is written in terms of it without fractions.

whyCorrect: The slope is \(\frac{-7-9}{6-(-2)}=\frac{-16}{8}=-2\), so the line is y − 9 = −2(x + 2), that is y = −2x + 5. Crossing the x-axis means y = 0, giving 0 = −2x + 5 and x = 2.5.
commonMistakes: Setting x = 0 instead of y = 0 and reporting 5, which is the y-intercept.
tips: The x-axis is the line y = 0; substitute 0 for y and solve for x.

whyCorrect: Put every length in centimetres first: the trough is 200 cm long. The trapezium's area is \(\frac{40+60}{2}\times 30=50\times 30=1{,}500\) square centimetres, so the volume is 1,500 × 200 = 300,000 cubic centimetres. Dividing by 1,000 gives 300 litres.
commonMistakes: Leaving the length as 2 and multiplying 1,500 × 2, which mixes metres with centimetres and gives an answer 100 times too small.
tips: Convert all lengths to one unit before computing a volume, and convert to litres only at the end.

whyCorrect: Write the system as 3h + 2t = 96 and 5h + 4t = 178. Doubling the first gives 6h + 4t = 192, and subtracting the second leaves h = 14. Substituting back, 3(14) + 2t = 96, so 2t = 54 and t = 27.

whyWrong.A: 14 is the bronze used by one handbell, the variable you eliminate on the way to the answer.
whyWrong.B: 21 for a tower bell forces h = 18, and then 5(18) + 4(21) = 174, not 178.
whyWrong.C: 24 for a tower bell forces h = 16, and then 5(16) + 4(24) = 176, two kilograms short of 178.

commonMistakes: Solving the system correctly and reporting the first variable you found.
tips: Scale one equation so a variable's coefficients match, then subtract — and check your pair in the equation you did not use to solve.

whyCorrect: Let the soprano section be s. Then the altos are s + 6 and the tenors are \(\frac{s}{2}\), and the three add to 96: \(s+(s+6)+\frac{s}{2}=96\). That is 2.5s + 6 = 96, so 2.5s = 90 and s = 36. The tenor section is \(\frac{36}{2}=18\).

whyWrong.B: 24 is 96 ÷ 4, splitting the choir into equal parts. With 24 tenors the sopranos would be 48 and the altos 54, a total of 126.
whyWrong.C: 36 is the soprano section, not the tenor section — halve it before answering.
whyWrong.D: 42 is the alto section (36 + 6).

tips: Define the variable as the section every other section is described against — here the sopranos — so both other sections are easy to write.

whyCorrect: The level fell 412 − 328 = 84 centimetres between day 5 and day 17, a span of 12 days, so it falls 84 ÷ 12 = 7 centimetres per day. From 328 down to 300 is another 28 centimetres, and 28 ÷ 7 = 4 days, so the level reaches 300 on day 17 + 4 = 21.

whyWrong.A: 19 comes from a rate of 14 cm per day (dividing 84 by 6 rather than by the 12 days between readings). On day 19 the true level is 314 cm.
whyWrong.C: On day 24 the model gives 328 − 7(7) = 279 cm, well past 300.
whyWrong.D: On day 28 the model gives 251 cm. Overshooting like this means too many days were added to the day-17 reading.

tips: Subtract the day numbers, not just the levels, to get the rate — the readings are 12 days apart, not 12 units of anything else.

whyCorrect: Find r first: 141 = 45 + 24r gives 24r = 96 and r = 4 dollars per mile. Then a 38-mile delivery costs 45 + 4(38) = 45 + 152 = $197. Equivalently, 38 is 14 miles further, and 14 × $4 = $56, so 141 + 56 = $197.

whyWrong.A: $173 is 45 + 4(32), pricing only 32 miles.
whyWrong.B: $189 is 141 + 48, adding for 12 extra miles instead of the 14 between 24 and 38.
whyWrong.D: $211 is 141 + 70, charging the 14 extra miles at $5 each rather than the $4 the first delivery implies.

tips: Solve for the constant with the delivery you know, then use the full rule — or work from the difference in miles, which skips the $45 entirely.

whyCorrect: The rate is constant: from 2 to 5 hours the depth rises 61 − 34 = 27 metres in 3 hours, that is 9 metres per hour (the 9-to-12-hour rows agree: 27 metres in 3 hours). From hour 12 at 124 metres, hour 20 is 8 hours later, so the depth is 124 + 9(8) = 196 metres.

whyWrong.A: 169 is 124 + 9(5), advancing only 5 hours past hour 12.
whyWrong.B: 178 is 124 + 9(6), advancing 6 hours.
whyWrong.C: 187 is 124 + 9(7) — one hour short of the 8 hours between hour 12 and hour 20.

tips: Build the rule once, \(d=16+9t\), and substitute; it removes the counting error that comes from stepping forward row by row.

whyCorrect: The 8 required frame repairs use 8 × 14 = 112 minutes, leaving 300 − 112 = 188 minutes. Each cleaning takes 26 minutes, and 188 ÷ 26 = 7.23, so she can finish 7 cleanings (182 minutes) but not an eighth.

whyWrong.A: 6 cleanings use 156 minutes and leave 32 minutes spare — enough for another cleaning, so 6 is not the greatest.
whyWrong.C: 8 cleanings need 208 minutes, which with the 112 minutes of repairs totals 320 minutes, over the 300 available.
whyWrong.D: 9 cleanings need 234 minutes, totalling 346 minutes.

commonMistakes: Rounding 7.23 up. A partly finished cleaning does not count.
tips: Subtract the fixed obligation first, then divide, and round down.

whyCorrect: Let the country-road speed be c, so the motorway speed is c + 6. Distance is speed times time: 3c + 2(c + 6) = 152. That gives 5c + 12 = 152, so 5c = 140 and c = 28.

whyWrong.A: 24 km/h gives 3(24) + 2(30) = 132 kilometres, 20 short of 152.
whyWrong.B: 26 km/h gives 3(26) + 2(32) = 142 kilometres, still 10 short.
whyWrong.D: 34 is the motorway speed, 28 + 6. The question asks about the country roads.

commonMistakes: Averaging: 152 ÷ 5 = 30.4 is the average speed over the whole trip, not either leg.
tips: Write a distance term for each leg (speed × its own time) and add them to the total.

whyCorrect: Factor the numerator so that (3x − 5) appears: \(6x^{2}+11x-35=(3x-5)(2x+7)\), since the cross terms give 21x − 10x = 11x. Cancelling the common factor leaves 2x + 7.

whyWrong.A: \(2x-7\) has the sign flipped; \((3x-5)(2x-7)=6x^{2}-31x+35\), which is not the numerator.
whyWrong.C: \(3x+7\) multiplied by (3x − 5) gives \(9x^{2}+6x-35\) — the leading term must be \(6x^{2}\), so the other factor starts with 2x.
whyWrong.D: \(6x+7\) multiplied by (3x − 5) gives \(18x^{2}\) as the leading term, three times too large.

tips: Check a division of polynomials by multiplying your answer back by the divisor; the leading and constant terms alone catch most errors.

whyCorrect: The parabola opens downward (the \(n^{2}\) coefficient is negative), so the greatest yield is at the vertex: \(n=-\frac{448}{2(-8)}=\frac{448}{16}=28\). The yield there is Y(28) = 5,772 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: Y(12) = 3,724 kilograms, well below the maximum.
whyWrong.B: 16 is 448 ÷ 28 rather than \(\frac{448}{2(8)}\); Y(16) = 4,620 kilograms.
whyWrong.C: Y(24) = 5,644 kilograms. Close to the peak is not at the peak — the vertex is the only maximum.

tips: Use \(-\frac{b}{2a}\) and be careful that a = −8, so the two negatives cancel.

whyCorrect: Set the model equal to 50: \(6{,}250\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{d}=50\), so \(\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{d}=\frac{50}{6{,}250}=\frac{1}{125}\). Since \(125=5^{3}\), the exponent is d = 3.

whyWrong.B: After 4 days the activity is \(\frac{6{,}250}{625}=10\) becquerels, already past 50.
whyWrong.C: After 5 days it is 2 becquerels.
whyWrong.D: After 6 days it is 0.4 becquerels.

commonMistakes: Dividing 6,250 by 50 to get 125 and then answering 125 or 5 — the 125 is the factor of decrease, and you still need the power of 5 that produces it.
tips: Rewrite the required factor as a power of the base; \(\frac{1}{125}=\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{3}\) reads the exponent off directly.

whyCorrect: Setting the two equal gives \(x^{2}+4x-12=3x+8\), which rearranges to \(x^{2}+x-20=0\). That factors as (x + 5)(x − 4) = 0, so the x-coordinates are −5 and 4 and their product is −20. (You can read it off without factoring: for \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\), the product of the roots is \(\frac{c}{a}=-20\).)

whyWrong.B: −5 is one of the two x-coordinates, not the product of both.
whyWrong.C: −1 is the sum of the roots, \(-\frac{b}{a}\).
whyWrong.D: 20 has the right size but the wrong sign; one root is negative and the other positive, so their product must be negative.

tips: Move everything to one side first — the product and sum of the roots come straight from \(\frac{c}{a}\) and \(-\frac{b}{a}\) of that combined equation.

whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by 3 to clear the fraction: 3w = 5g − 14. Add 14 to both sides, 3w + 14 = 5g, then divide by 5 to get \(g=\frac{3w+14}{5}\).

whyWrong.B: Subtracts the 14 instead of adding it. The original has −14 on the right, so undoing it means adding.
whyWrong.C: Swaps the roles of the 3 and the 5 — the 3 was the denominator in the original, so it multiplies w, and the 5 was attached to g, so it divides.
whyWrong.D: Stops before dividing by 5, giving 5g rather than g.

tips: Clear the denominator first, then undo the addition, then undo the multiplication.

whyWrong.A: 180 scales the power in direct proportion to the speed, \(108\times\frac{10}{6}\). The model cubes the speed, so power grows much faster than that.
whyWrong.B: 300 scales by the square, \(108\times\left(\frac{10}{6}\right)^{2}\), missing one factor of the speed ratio.
whyWrong.D: 540 would require c = 0.54, but \(c=\frac{108}{216}=0.5\).

commonMistakes: Trying to find c without cubing: \(\frac{108}{6}=18\) is not c.
tips: Either solve for the constant, or scale by the ratio raised to the same power: \(108\times\left(\frac{10}{6}\right)^{3}=500\).

whyCorrect: Growing by 15% multiplies the area by 1.15 each week, so after 5 weeks it is \(2{,}000(1.15)^{5}\). Since \((1.15)^{5}\approx 2.0114\), the area is about 4,022.7, which rounds to 4,023 square metres.

whyWrong.A: 3,530 is roughly the simple-growth figure 2,000(1 + 0.15 × 5) = 3,500, which adds 15% of the original area each week. Compounding applies the 15% to the larger area each time.
whyWrong.C: 4,600 is 2,300 × 2 — one week of growth followed by a doubling, which is not what a 15% weekly rate does.
whyWrong.D: 5,000 is 2.5 times the starting area; it comes from rounding \((1.15)^{5}\) up to 2.5 instead of using 2.0114.

tips: For repeated percent growth use \(A_{0}(1+r)^{t}\) and keep the full power until the final rounding.

whyCorrect: 96 metres of cloth is 96 ÷ 4 = 24 lots of 4 metres, and each lot needs 7 grams, so 24 × 7 = 168 grams. At $3 per gram, the cost is 168 × 3 = $504.

whyWrong.A: $336 pays for only 112 grams of madder, two-thirds of what the job needs.
whyWrong.B: $420 pays for 140 grams, still short of the 168 grams required.
whyWrong.D: 672 is 96 × 7, the gram figure you get by skipping the division by 4 — and it is a mass, not a price.

tips: Do the chain in order: metres to grams using the ratio, then grams to dollars using the price, checking the units at each step.

whyCorrect: A 20% cut multiplies by 0.80 and a 35% rise on the reduced fare multiplies by 1.35, so the original fare f satisfies f(0.80)(1.35) = 54, that is 1.08f = 54 and f = $50. Check: $50 falls to $40, then rises to $54.

whyWrong.A: $40 is 54 ÷ 1.35, which undoes only the autumn rise. Starting from $40 the two changes give $43.20.
whyWrong.B: $45 comes from dividing by 1.2, treating the pair of changes as a single 20% rise. Starting from $45 the fare would end at $48.60.
whyWrong.C: Starting from $48 the fare goes to $38.40 and then to $51.84, not $54.

commonMistakes: Adding the percentages: −20% and +35% do not combine to +15%, because the 35% is applied to the already-reduced fare.
tips: Multiply the two factors, 0.80 × 1.35 = 1.08, to get the single net multiplier, then divide the final amount by it.

whyCorrect: Total the columns: 2015 gives 40 + 55 + 35 + 70 = 200 pairs and 2022 gives 52 + 70 + 48 + 80 = 250 pairs. The increase is 50 pairs, and the percent increase is \(\frac{50}{200}=0.25\), or 25%.

whyWrong.A: 20% is \(\frac{50}{250}\), dividing the increase by the new total. Percent increase is always measured against the original.
whyWrong.C: 50 is the increase in pairs, not a percentage.
whyWrong.D: 125% is \(\frac{250}{200}\) — the new total as a percent of the old one. The increase is that minus 100%.

tips: Percent increase is (new − old) ÷ old; if you compute new ÷ old, subtract 1 at the end.

whyCorrect: Work with totals. All 14 members mass 14 × 78 = 1,092 kilograms and the 6 lightweights mass 6 × 62 = 372 kilograms, so the other 8 mass 1,092 − 372 = 720 kilograms. Their mean is 720 ÷ 8 = 90 kilograms.
commonMistakes: Assuming the two group means average to the overall mean; they only would if the groups were the same size, and here 6 and 8 differ.
tips: Convert every mean into a total (mean × count) before combining or splitting groups.

whyCorrect: Let the smallest angle be s. Then the largest is 3s and the third is s + 20, and the three sum to 180: s + 3s + (s + 20) = 180. That gives 5s = 160 and s = 32, so the largest angle is 3(32) = 96 degrees.

whyWrong.A: 32 is the smallest angle, the value of s itself.
whyWrong.B: 52 is the third angle, s + 20.
whyWrong.C: 64 is 2(32), doubling the smallest angle instead of tripling it.

commonMistakes: Stopping once you have solved for s. Check which angle the question names before you answer.
tips: Verify by adding: 32 + 96 + 52 = 180.

whyCorrect: The belt is the hypotenuse and the 15-metre height is the side opposite the 30-degree angle, so \(\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{15}{L}\). Since \(\sin 30^{\circ}=0.5\), the belt is L = 30 metres long. At 2 metres per second that takes 30 ÷ 2 = 15 seconds.

whyWrong.A: 7.5 divides the 15-metre height by the speed, using the vertical rise as though it were the belt's length. The slanted belt is always longer than the height it climbs.
whyWrong.C: 30 is the length of the belt in metres, not the time — divide by the 2 metres per second.
whyWrong.D: 60 multiplies the 30-metre belt by the speed instead of dividing by it.

tips: At a 30-degree incline the hypotenuse is exactly twice the vertical rise, which is a fast check on the belt's length.

whyCorrect: Volume scales as the cube of the linear scale factor. A model at \(\frac{1}{4}\) of the linear size has \(\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{64}\) of the volume, so the model contains \(\frac{448}{64}=7\) cubic feet.
commonMistakes: Dividing by 4 (112) or by 16 (28). Lengths divide by 4, areas by 16, volumes by 64.
tips: Match the power to the dimension: length is the first power, area the square, volume the cube.

whyCorrect: At the same moment the sun's angle is the same, so the height-to-shadow ratio is the same for both objects: \(\frac{2.4}{1.8}=\frac{h}{31.5}\). Since \(\frac{2.4}{1.8}=\frac{4}{3}\), the spire is \(\frac{4}{3}(31.5)=42\) metres tall.
commonMistakes: Inverting the ratio and computing \(\frac{3}{4}(31.5)=23.6\). The pole is taller than its shadow, so the spire must be taller than its shadow too.
tips: Set up the proportion as (height)/(shadow) for each object, then check the answer is on the sensible side of the shadow length.

whyCorrect: Each book uses the same 8 signatures, so the number of books is 152 ÷ 8 = 19. Check: 19 × 8 = 152.

whyWrong.A: 17 books would use 136 signatures, 16 fewer than were used.
whyWrong.B: 18 books would use 144 signatures, leaving 8 unaccounted for — exactly one more book's worth.
whyWrong.D: 21 books would use 168 signatures, more than the bindery had.

tips: Multiply your quotient back by the divisor; if it does not rebuild the total, the division was wrong.

whyCorrect: Take the supplies out first: 23 − 5 = 18 kilograms remain. Splitting 18 kilograms equally among 3 bags gives 18 ÷ 3 = 6 kilograms each.

whyWrong.A: 5 is the mass left at the hut, not the mass in a bag.
whyWrong.C: 7.5 kilograms per bag would mean 22.5 kilograms were divided, but only 18 kilograms are carried on.
whyWrong.D: 9 is 18 ÷ 2, dividing the load between two bags instead of three.

commonMistakes: Dividing the full 23 kilograms and then subtracting; the 5 kilograms comes off the whole load before the split.
tips: Handle the subtraction and the division in the order the sentence describes them.

whyCorrect: The hourly part is 13 × 5 = $65, and the $18 launch fee is paid once. The total is 65 + 18 = $83.

whyWrong.A: 65 is the hourly charge alone, with the launch fee left out.
whyWrong.B: 78 is 18 + 12(5), using $12 an hour instead of $13.
whyWrong.D: 95 overcharges by $12. The fee is added once, not scaled with the hours: 18 + 13(5) = 83.

tips: A one-off fee is added at the end; only the per-hour rate gets multiplied by the time.

whyCorrect: The bin starts at 240 kilograms and loses 15 kilograms per week, so after w weeks it has lost 15w kilograms in total. What remains is 240 − 15w.

whyWrong.B: \(240w-15\) multiplies the starting mass by the weeks, which would make the bin grow, and subtracts 15 only once.
whyWrong.C: \(15w-240\) has the terms reversed and is negative for the first sixteen weeks.
whyWrong.D: 225w is 240 − 15 worked out first and then multiplied by w. The subtraction has to happen after 15 is multiplied by the number of weeks.

tips: Model a steady loss as (starting amount) − (rate)(time); only the rate carries the variable.

whyCorrect: "No more than 8" means 8 is allowed but nothing above it, which is \(p\le 8\).

whyWrong.A: \(p<8\) rules out a full load of 8 passengers, which the notice permits.
whyWrong.B: \(p\ge 8\) points the wrong way and would allow 9 or more.
whyWrong.D: \(p>8\) allows only the numbers the limit forbids.

tips: "No more than" and "at most" both mean \(\le\); "fewer than" means <.

whyCorrect: The traveller spent 50 − 14 = $36 on tickets. At $4 each, that is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 tickets.

whyWrong.A: 8 tickets cost $32 and would leave $18 in change, not $14.
whyWrong.C: 11 tickets cost $44 and would leave $6 in change.
whyWrong.D: 12 is 50 ÷ 4 rounded down, which spends the whole note and ignores the $14 that came back.

tips: Find the amount actually spent (note minus change) before dividing by the unit price.

whyCorrect: In \(D(t)=560-70t\) the 70 is multiplied by t and subtracted, so each additional hour removes 70 kilometres from the distance still to go. That is the rate of decrease — the driving speed, expressed as the drop in remaining distance per hour.

whyWrong.A: The total distance is 560, the value of D when t = 0.
whyWrong.B: The whole drive takes 560 ÷ 70 = 8 hours, which comes from setting D(t) = 0, not from the 70 itself.
whyWrong.C: The distance remaining after one hour is D(1) = 560 − 70 = 490 kilometres.

tips: In \(y=b+mt\), the constant b is the starting value and the coefficient m is the change per unit of time.

whyCorrect: Add the two expressions and combine like terms separately: the m terms give 5m + 3m = 8m, and the constants give −8 + 14 = 6. The total is 8m + 6.

whyWrong.B: \(8m-6\) comes from −8 − 14, subtracting the border's constant instead of adding it.
whyWrong.C: \(2m+6\) subtracts the m terms (5m − 3m); the question asks for the total, so they add.
whyWrong.D: \(8m+22\) treats the −8 as +8, giving 8 + 14 = 22. The letters use \(5m-8\) grams, so that constant is negative.

tips: Combine like terms in two separate columns — variable terms and constants — to keep the signs straight.

whyCorrect: Distribute the 3 to both terms inside the parentheses: 3(2x) = 6x and 3(5) = 15, giving 6x + 15.

whyWrong.A: \(6x+5\) multiplies only the 2x and leaves the 5 untouched.
whyWrong.B: \(2x+15\) multiplies only the 5.
whyWrong.C: \(5x+6\) swaps the two results; 3 × 2 = 6 belongs with x and 3 × 5 = 15 is the constant.

tips: Every term inside the parentheses gets multiplied — check by substituting x = 1: 3(7) = 21, and 6(1) + 15 = 21.

whyCorrect: Substitute n = 4 into \(3n^{2}\). Square first: \(4^{2}=16\). Then multiply by 3: 3 × 16 = 48 tiles.

whyWrong.A: 24 is 3 × 4 × 2, multiplying by the exponent instead of squaring.
whyWrong.B: 36 is \(3^{2}\times 4\), squaring the coefficient instead of n.
whyWrong.D: 144 is \((3\times 4)^{2}\), squaring the whole product. The exponent applies only to n.

tips: Exponents bind tighter than multiplication, so square n before touching the 3.

whyCorrect: Set the rule equal to 8: \(\frac{x^{2}}{50}=8\). Multiply both sides by 50 to get \(x^{2}=400\), then take the positive square root: x = 20 centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 16 is 2 × 8, doubling the number of people rather than solving for x. A 16 cm pan serves \(\frac{256}{50}\approx 5\) people.
whyWrong.C: 25 is half of 50; a 25 cm pan serves \(\frac{625}{50}=12.5\) people.
whyWrong.D: 40 comes from mis-rooting \(x^{2}=400\); \(\sqrt{400}=20\), and a 40 cm pan would serve 32 people.

tips: Clear the denominator first, then take the square root — and check by substituting your value back into the rule.
